Flipping Items Simultaneously II

InvariantsParityAlgebra
Game: A ring of red circles has one blue one. Make the circle next to the arrow the only blue one.
How to play: Press a circle: it and the next few circles clockwise swap colours. Choose how many with M, and how many circles with N.

Look for the math

N circles stand in a ring, one of them blue. Each click changes the colour of M neighbouring circles. Can you move the blue colour to the circle the arrow points at, leaving all the others red? For N = 12 and M = 3, 4 or 6 you cannot.

An invariant when M divides N

Tick Solution helper (it is offered when M divides N). Circles whose place leaves the remainder 0 or M − 1 on division by M get a green centre. Among any M circles in a row there are exactly two marked ones, so every click changes the colour of exactly two marked circles. Write 1 for red and −1 for blue: the product of the numbers on the marked circles starts at −1 and stays −1. Both the starting blue circle is marked and the target is not (when M is at least 3), so all-marked-red is impossible. The logic test did not only rely on the proof: it searched every state reachable from the start, for every N up to 16, and the target was never among them when M ≥ 3 divides N.

For M = 2 every circle is marked, the argument breaks, and the target can be reached by clicking neighbouring pairs; the page's proof says “M divides N” but needs M ≥ 3.

Other pairs of M and N

The page asks what can be said about other pairs. The test solved the puzzle over the field of two elements (a click twice undoes itself, so each circle is clicked 0 or 1 times) for every N up to 60 and every M below N, and compared with a rule: the target can be reached exactly when gcd(M, N) = 1, or gcd(M, N) = 2 and M is 2 more than a multiple of 4. The test also checked every pair in the applet’s range against a search of the whole state graph, and replayed every solution it found. The reason for the impossible cases is the same kind of invariant: with g = gcd(M, N), a click changes M/g circles in each of the g classes of circles that are alike modulo g; the start and target blue circles are in different classes, and a class pattern that cannot be fixed is an obstruction. “Show a solution” plays out a way when there is one.

Try N = 7, M = 3, then N = 10, M = 6, then N = 10, M = 4. Which can be solved?

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
